generatedProse.concept-context: In any subject, slides can carry a lot: data, quotations, tables, lists. The temptation is to put all of it on the screen and read it out. An effective visual aid does the opposite. It shows one clear image or a few key words that support your spoken point, so the audience follows your argument rather than decoding a crowded slide. The talk carries the thinking; the slides serve it.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students designing slides for the same presentation.

Student A fills each slide with full paragraphs and every table from the source, then reads them out word for word. The slides are crowded and hard to read from the back. The audience reads ahead and stops listening, and Student A runs over time. The slides have taken over the talk. This is the most common presentation error: the overloaded slide, read aloud.

Student B puts only one clear image or a few key words on each slide, enough to cue a point, and speaks around them. The slides are easy to read and support what is said rather than repeating it. The audience listens, and the talk keeps to time. The slides help the argument instead of carrying it.

Both students had the same material to present. Only Student B designed slides that support the talk rather than crowd it out.
generatedProse.summary: Visual aids are there to support what you say, not to replace it. An effective slide is clear and uncluttered; the common errors, above all the overloaded slide read aloud, follow from forgetting that. You can now identify the features of an effective visual aid, tell a clear slide from an overloaded one, and recognise a common error and how to avoid it. With what a presentation is, how to plan and structure one, and how to design its slides, you have the foundations to build a presentation of your own.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Student B's slides better than Student A's?

items.text: They used one clear image or a few key words to support each point, not full paragraphs and every table.
They used more slides than Student A's.
They used brighter colours on every slide.
They repeated the spoken words exactly on each slide.

feedback.correct: That's right. Spare slides that support the spoken point are the better design.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Student B's slides did with text and data.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Student B's slides used one clear image or a few key words to support each point. More slides, brighter colours or repeated text do not make a slide effective.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline.
